title: Ear-warming neckwarmer
subtitle: A short tube that covers the neck and sits high enough to warm the ears.
excerpt: A neckwarmer knitted in the round in 2x2 rib on 5 mm needles with worsted-weight yarn, finishing at 50 cm circumference and 22 cm tall. The extra height relative to a standard cowl means the top edge can be folded out to cover the ears while the bottom edge rests at the base of the neck.
sourceNotes: Short ribbed neckwarmers and neck muffatees appear in Weldon's Practical Knitter series (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive, as well as in Cornelia Mee, A Manual of Knitting and Crochet (1846), Internet Archive.
heroPrompt: A finished ear-warming neckwarmer in forest green worsted-weight yarn, photographed on a plain mannequin with the top edge folded out to show how it covers the ears, the bottom edge resting at the collar.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rib pattern alternating two knit stitches with two purl stitches on every row or round, giving a stretchy, reversible fabric. In the round the pattern is simply K2, P2 on every round.
Knitting a small circumference in the round on one long circular needle by pulling a loop of cable through the stitches at the halfway point.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.
A bind-off producing a looser, more elastic edge than the standard bind-off, essential on rib that needs to stretch over the head.

content.text: This is a neckwarmer knitted in the round in
2x2 rib

on 5 mm needles with worsted-weight yarn, finishing at 50 cm circumference and 22 cm tall. The tube is tall enough that the top edge, when folded out, covers the ears. The bottom edge sits at the base of the neck or slightly above the collarbone. In 2x2 rib the tube stretches to fit comfortably over the head for pulling on, and springs back to 50 cm when worn.
In-the-round construction was chosen because a seamless tube is the simplest possible neckwarmer construction and avoids any seam that might irritate the neck. The
magic loop
technique on an 80 cm circular needle handles the 68 cast-on stitches easily. The finished neckwarmer needs about 130 m (approximately 80 g) of worsted-weight yarn.
What you need

items.name: Worsted-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any worsted-weight yarn. Wool gives the best warmth and stretch retention.

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch in the round on 5 mm needles, blocked. In 2x2 rib relaxed in the round the gauge is approximately 14 sts per 10 cm. Swatch the rib in the round and measure unstretched. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished circumference by approximately 3.6 cm at this stitch count. Because the rib is very stretchy, a slightly larger or smaller circumference will still fit comfortably over most adult heads (which average 55 to 58 cm).
Stitches used
K (knit), P (purl). In the round, 2x2 rib is simply *K2, P2; repeat from * to end on every round. There is no wrong-side round.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 68 stitches on the needle. The stitch count must be a multiple of 4 for 2x2 rib; 68 stitches at 14 sts per 10 cm relaxed gives approximately 48.6 cm, which stretches comfortably to 50 cm when worn. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 68 stitches: (15.7 x 68) / 10 + 15 = 106.8 + 15 = about 122 cm. Leave at least 122 cm of tail.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 68 stitches on the needle. Join to work in the round without twisting. Place a stitch marker.
Body
Every round: *K2, P2; repeat from * to end. (68 sts)
Repeat this round until the neckwarmer measures 22 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway mark (approximately round 24 of 48 body rounds), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at round 24 you should have 68 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a
stretchy bind-off
in pattern (K2tog on knit stitches, P2tog on purl stitches before binding off each pair). Both the cast-on and bind-off edges need to stretch to 58 cm or more to pass over an adult head.
Common faults

Neckwarmer will not stretch over the head. Either the bind-off or cast-on edge is too tight. Test by stretching each edge to at least 58 cm before finishing. If a bind-off row is too tight, rip back and repeat using needles two sizes larger.

Top edge not reaching the ears. The 22 cm tube folds approximately 5 to 7 cm over the top when worn, leaving about 15 cm below the fold at the neckline. If the ears are still cold, knit the tube to 26 or 27 cm before binding off.
Twisted join. Lay the full cast-on row flat and confirm no stitches are twisted before joining the first round. A twist in 68 stitches of worsted yarn is harder to spot than in a small stitch count.
Finishing
Weave in both tails at the cast-on join and bind-off edge. The rib does not need blocking. The tube can be folded double at the cast-on edge before wearing to make a shorter, double-thickness cowl.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry. The rib will recover its stretch after washing and drying flat.
What to try next
The ribbed cowl is the same 2x2 rib tube at a wider circumference. The basic cowl replaces the rib with stocking stitch, which gives a smoother look but does not stretch as far over the head.
